knowledge_weighting.method: entry-weighted mean of O*NET 31.0 importance (Scale IM): entry targets weight 2; other linked occupations in Job Zone 4 or 5 (or the entry targets' Job Zone) weight 1; Manager, Chief, Postsecondary-faculty, All Other, Supervisor, Director and Treasurers and Controllers titles, and non-target occupations in other Job Zones, weight 0
knowledge_weighting.note: top_knowledge/top_skills are the unweighted mean over all linked occupations (kept for comparison); the outline uses the entry-weighted lists.

skipped_knowledge.reason: service and client-relations knowledge; the outline leaves it to internships, part-time work and the practice tasks rather than a course slot
management and planning knowledge matters most after several years of experience, so the outline gives it no course slot (a management elective is optional)
teaching and training others is built through presenting, tutoring and peer teaching in projects rather than a dedicated course

outline_elements.rule: English Language is placed in Year 1 general education; workplace and management elements (Customer and Personal Service, Administrative, Clerical, Administration and Management, Personnel and Human Resources, Education and Training) get no course slot unless the major's CIP series is about them; the next three elements go to Year 2 and up to three more (ordered by importance to the entry targets) to Year 3; if fewer than two remain for Year 3, knowledge rated at least 2.5 for the entry targets fills it

method.supervisory_tasks: task statement matches a supervisory/managerial pattern (supervise, provide supervision, direct and coordinate, direct the work/activities/staff of, manage staff/personnel/employees/workers/teams, oversee the work/staff, hire, subordinates, assign work to, evaluate the work/performance of, train and supervise); 'under supervision' does not count

quality_flags.note: Authored tier: entry targets and practice tasks were chosen and reviewed per major, so the generated-tier plausibility flags are not applied. Informational only: cited tasks whose O*NET statement is supervisory are listed; their authored scenarios say when they are practice for a later or graduate role.

entry_targets.title: Software Quality Assurance Analysts and Testers

entry_target_basis: Job Zone 4 linked occupations (excluding Manager/Chief/Postsecondary/All Other/Supervisor/Director/Treasurers and Controllers titles), ranked by similarity of their O*NET knowledge-importance profile to the average profile of the eligible linked occupations (Pearson correlation), base O*NET-SOC .00 codes first; then a documented DreamCo manual override (authored/target_overrides.json) changed the rule output (15-1253.00, 15-1212.00, 15-1243.00) to 15-1252.00, 15-1253.00, 15-1212.00

entry_target_review.reason: Software Developers is the most common bachelor's-level destination for Computer Science graduates and was missing because the knowledge-profile ranking favored QA, security and database roles. Database Architects was dropped: architect roles typically expect several years of database administration or development experience, so it is a mid-career rather than a new-graduate target. Software QA and Information Security Analysts are kept as realistic Job Zone 4 entry roles.

practice_tasks.prompt: DreamCo-original practice prompt. A student-run campus food-ordering app is about to ship a 'split the bill' feature that lets up to six friends share one order, each paying by card or meal-plan credit. Write the test plan for this feature: scope and out-of-scope items, at least eight named test scenarios (include rounding of odd cents, one payer's card being declined, and a friend leaving the group mid-checkout), which scenarios you would automate versus run by hand, test data you need, and the exit criteria for release.

rubric.description: Scenarios cover the normal path, boundary values (1 and 6 payers, odd-cent totals) and failure paths (declined card, timeout, member leaving), not only happy paths.
The split between automated and manual tests is justified by repeatability, risk and cost, and the test data needed is stated concretely.
Exit criteria are measurable (e.g. zero open severity-1 defects, all payment-path tests passing) and say who signs off.

reference_answer_outline: Scope statement naming the split-bill flow, payment providers and meal-plan ledger; excludes unrelated menu features.
Scenario table with ID, preconditions, steps and expected result; includes the cent-rounding rule (who absorbs the leftover cent).
Automates calculation and API-level payment tests; keeps exploratory and multi-device UX checks manual.
Lists test accounts, sandbox cards that decline, and a meal-plan balance near zero.
Exit criteria with severity thresholds and a named approver.

practice_tasks.prompt: DreamCo-original practice prompt. A 40-person food-bank nonprofit just had a volunteer coordinator's email account taken over through a fake 'shared document' link, and the attacker emailed donors asking for gift cards. Design a 30-minute security-awareness session for staff and regular volunteers: three learning objectives, the agenda minute by minute, one realistic hands-on exercise built from this incident (no real victim names), and how you will measure whether behavior changed 60 days later.

rubric.description: Content suits non-technical staff and volunteers, uses the real incident pattern, and avoids jargon or blame.
Objectives translate into specific behaviors (checking sender domains, reporting suspicious mail, using MFA) that the exercise actually practices.
The 60-day measure is concrete, such as a simulated phishing click rate or report rate compared with a baseline.

reference_answer_outline: Objectives: recognize credential-phishing cues, report quickly through one named channel, turn on MFA.
Agenda: 5 min story of the incident, 10 min cue spotting, 10 min hands-on inbox triage exercise, 5 min MFA setup check.
Exercise uses three sanitized sample emails, one legitimate and two malicious.
Follow-up: simulated phish at day 45 to 60, compare click and report rates with a pre-session baseline.
Notes privacy: individual results are not used for discipline.

practice_tasks.prompt: DreamCo-original practice prompt. Your registrar's office runs a five-year-old Python script that exports course enrollments to a CSV for the state reporting portal. Since enrollment doubled it takes 40 minutes and times out, it crashes on student names with accented characters, and the portal is moving from CSV upload to a JSON API next term. Write a change proposal: diagnose the likely causes of each problem, the code changes you would make, how you will prove the new version produces the same records as the old one, and a rollback plan.

rubric.description: Each symptom gets a plausible technical cause (e.g. row-by-row queries, wrong text encoding) and a way to confirm it, such as profiling or a failing test case.
Changes are scoped and safe: performance fix, UTF-8 handling, and an output layer that supports both CSV and the new API without rewriting everything.
Equivalence is proven with a record-level comparison on real-sized data, and rollback is concrete.

reference_answer_outline: Profile first; likely N+1 database queries or loading everything into memory; fix with batched queries or a single join.
Encoding crash: read and write explicitly as UTF-8; add test names with accents and non-Latin scripts.
Separate data extraction from output formatting so a JSON API client can be added beside the CSV writer.
Verification: run old and new on the same snapshot and diff record counts and field values.
Rollback: keep the old script deployable and switch back with one configuration flag.

practice_tasks.prompt: DreamCo-original practice prompt. A web app used by 3,000 club members is replacing its password-hashing library (from an old salted SHA-1 scheme to bcrypt) and will rehash each password when that user next logs in. Before deployment, write the regression checklist you would run: what must still work, the specific edge cases for users who have not logged in since the change, the security checks, the performance check on the login endpoint, and the go/no-go rule.

rubric.description: Covers migration edge cases: old-hash users, users mid-reset, accounts with very long or Unicode passwords, and the first login after deploy.
Each item has a pass condition, such as login latency under a stated threshold or no plaintext passwords in logs.
A clear go/no-go rule with what happens if a check fails, including a rollback path that does not lock users out.

reference_answer_outline: Core regressions: login, logout, password reset, account creation, session expiry.
Migration cases: legacy-hash user logs in and is rehashed; reset link issued before deploy still works or fails safely.
Security: confirm the bcrypt cost factor, no hashes or passwords in logs, rate limiting still on.
Performance: measure p95 login latency before and after; bcrypt cost tuned to stay within target.
Go/no-go: all severity-1 checks pass; rollback keeps both hash verifiers so no user is locked out.

practice_tasks.prompt: DreamCo-original practice prompt. A three-office dental practice has bought two things: multi-factor authentication for its practice-management software, and a managed endpoint-protection service from an outside vendor. You are the security analyst coordinating the rollout over four weeks without disrupting patient scheduling. Write the coordination plan: who does what (practice staff, office managers, the MFA vendor, the endpoint vendor), the week-by-week schedule, how you will communicate with front-desk staff, and the three biggest rollout risks with mitigations.

rubric.description: Responsibilities of internal staff and each vendor are explicit, including who approves changes and who provides support at each office.
Sequencing protects clinic operations: pilot first, after-hours installs, and no MFA enforcement on a full patient day without fallback.
Risks are specific (lost phones, legacy imaging PCs, vendor delays) and each has a workable mitigation.

reference_answer_outline: RACI-style table: analyst coordinates, office managers schedule staff, vendors install and support.
Week 1 pilot at one office; weeks 2 and 3 roll out to the others; week 4 enforce MFA and review.
Front desk gets a one-page guide and a named on-call contact during the first enforced day.
Risks: shared front-desk logins, old imaging workstations unsupported by the agent, phones unavailable; mitigations include hardware tokens and exceptions logged with an expiry date.
Success measures: percentage of accounts enrolled and endpoint agents reporting.

practice_tasks.prompt: DreamCo-original practice prompt. The university library asks for a study-room booking app: students reserve rooms from their phones, staff can block rooms for events, no-shows are released after 15 minutes, and it must work with campus single sign-on. You have two part-time student developers for eight weeks and no budget for paid services beyond existing campus hosting. Write a one-page feasibility memo: the requirements you would confirm with users, a rough effort estimate per feature, what fits in eight weeks, what you would cut or defer, and your recommendation.

rubric.description: Distinguishes must-have from nice-to-have requirements and names open questions to confirm with students and staff.
Effort estimates are broken down by feature, include testing and SSO integration risk, and add up within the stated capacity.
Recommends a specific scope (build, reduce, or buy/adapt existing tool) with the trade-offs stated.

reference_answer_outline: Must-haves: SSO login, view availability, book and cancel, staff block-out; nice-to-have: notifications, analytics.
Open questions: booking limits per student, accessibility needs, room check-in method for no-show release.
Estimate in developer-weeks per feature, with SSO and testing called out; total compared with about 16 part-time developer-weeks.
Defer push notifications and analytics; consider an existing open-source booking system if SSO support exists.
Recommendation with a scope, a timeline and the main risk.
